This can make direct comparisons between older and newer films misleading because the purchasing power of money has changed over time. For example, if a movie made $100 million in 2000, and another made $100 million in 2010, the 2000 film might have been more successful in real terms because the cost of a movie ticket was much lower in 2000. To accurately compare the success of films across different eras, one would need to adjust the numbers for inflation. This involves converting the nominal box office earnings into real terms using a price index, such as the Consumer Price Index (CPI), to reflect the actual purchasing power of the money at the time of the film's release. However, such adjustments are not commonly done in the industry, and most comparisons are made using the raw, nominal figures. - I, J, K: Used in circular interpolation to define the center of a circle
- F: Feed rate
- S: Spindle speed
- T: Tool selection
